title: A Forgotten Encounter: A Case of Amebic Liver Abscess Mimicking Hepatic Malignancy in a Non-endemic Region
case_text:
A 58-year-old Hispanic female with a distant history of coccidioidomycosis diagnosed 20 years ago was admitted to Kern Medical Center through the emergency department (ED) with a one-month history of progressive right-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Her symptoms were accompanied by unintended weight loss of 15 pounds over the past month, intermittent subjective fevers, and chills for one week. Her family noted that she appeared increasingly frail, with a slow gait and significant weakness. Four months prior to admission, the patient attended the Kern County Fair, where she consumed nacho chips with cheese. This was followed by a one-month episode of diarrhea, after which her current symptoms gradually developed. She also reported a history of travel to Mexico one year ago. On admission, the patient presented with the following vital signs: blood pressure (BP) 100/60 mmHg, temperature 38.2 C, pulse 103/minute, and respiratory rate 28/minute. She was not in respiratory distress but had diminished breath sounds in the right lower lung and mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.
Laboratory results (Table 1) revealed elevated alkaline phosphatase (215 U/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (95 mm/h), and C-reactive protein (10.4 mg/dL); hemoglobin (Hb: 9.8 g/dL); normal white blood cell (WBC) count: 7.7 x 103/mcL; normal transaminases and bilirubin levels; normal creatinine level. Serology tests for coccidioidomycosis, HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B and C were negative.
A CT chest scan showed an elevated right hemidiaphragm with a heterogeneous 12 cm mass in the right hepatic lobe. An abdominal ultrasound (Figure 1) revealed a solid mass in the right hepatic lobe near the dome of the liver measuring 12.9 x 9.8 x 9.6 cm, raising concerns for malignancy.
A subsequent CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast (Figure 2) confirmed a lobulated, hypodense, non-cystic lesion measuring 14 x 10 x 13 cm. 
Tumor markers (AFP, CA 19-9, and CEA) were normal. Hydatid cysts were initially considered but ruled out based on the absence of cystic features on imaging. The patient underwent an ultrasound-guided liver biopsy, yielding approximately 500 mL of grayish purulent fluid. A drainage catheter was placed. Immediately post-procedure, she experienced a transient episode of hypotension and syncope, which resolved with intravenous fluids. Cultures of the aspirate and blood were negative for bacterial growth. Magnetic resonance imaging (Figure 3) performed two days after drainage showed a reduction in lesion size from 14 x 10 x 13 cm to 10.8 x 7.2 x 9.6 cm.
Given her travel history and clinical presentation, serology for Entamoeba histolytica was performed and came back positive for E. histolytica IgG antibodies. Based on the serological results, clinical symptoms, and imaging findings, a diagnosis of amebic liver abscess (ALA) was made.
The patient was started on oral metronidazole 750 mg three times daily, which led to rapid improvement in fever, weakness, and anorexia. She was hospitalized for ten days and discharged with continued oral metronidazole.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Amebiasis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: amebic liver abscess
